units.translation: 184. διερῇ πεφόρητο: διερή properly means the earth made wet by Zeus, from which also comes διαίνω, "I moisten." It is after the Homeric passage (Y 226-29): "but when they gambol over the grain-giving earth" and so forth.

185-88a. And two other sons: one was a son, the other Erginus was a descendant; Ancaeus was the son of Astypalaea, daughter of Phoenix, and Poseidon, while Erginus was the son of Clymenus, son of Presbon, and Buzyge, daughter of Lycus. Miletus, from whom the city Miletus is named, was the son of Euxantius, son of Minos; but some say he was the son of Apollo and Areia, daughter of Cleochus. He was called Miletus because he was hidden by his mother in a milax (yew). Others say that Miletus was founded by Sarpedon, son of Zeus, and named after the city in Crete. They say it was first called Pityussa, others Asteria, then Anactoria, then Miletus. And Aristocritus (fg 1 M. IV 334) says,

That Areia was the daughter of Cleochus, and from her and Apollo a child was born, and this child was exposed in a milax, and Cleochus took him up and named him Miletus from the milax. When he grew up and was envied by Minos, he withdrew to Samos, from which also a place there is called Miletus. And moving from Samos to Caria he founded a city, calling it Miletus after himself. Herodorus (31 fg 45 J.) bears witness.

b. 〈ὁ δ’ Ἰμβρασίης ἕδος Ἥρης Παρθενίην:〉 He means Samos. For Imbrasus is a river of Samos, which was renamed Parthenius because Hera was raised there while still a virgin. Callimachus (fg 213 Schn.) also mentions it. And Tarrhaeus says (fg 10 Linnenkugel): "Parthenia, Samos, was named after Parthenia, a woman of Samos." Lm (P)
